# Mahāsupinajātaka (Ja 77)

**ID:** Ja 77
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsupinajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsupinajātaka* (Ja 77) is an *eka-nipāta* story set at Jetavana concerning King Pasenadi of Kosala, who wakes in terror after experiencing sixteen ominous dreams [Norman 1983; Burlingame 1921]. Fearing impending danger to his life, kingdom, or wealth, the king consults his royal brahmins, who recommend an extensive animal sacrifice (*mahāyajña*) to avert disaster; however, Queen Mallikā advises him instead to consult the Buddha [Bareau 1993; Meisig 2010]. The Buddha interprets the sixteen dreams, reassuring the king and explaining that the visions portend social, moral, clerical, and political degeneration in distant future generations rather than immediate harm to him [Burlingame 1921; Appleton 2010; Meisig 2010]. From a textual and metrical standpoint, the canonical core consists of a single verse comprising seven *pādas* that list the dreams, though the *pratīka* oddly begins with the fourth *pāda*, an irregularity noticed by the commentators and linked to ancient transmission debates among the *jātaka-bhāṇakas* [Norman 1983].

Beyond the Pali commentary, the narrative has notable cross-tradition parallels and artistic representations. The introductory story corresponds to the final discourse of the Chinese *Ekottarāgama*, which transforms the narrative into an independent sūtra lacking a "story of the past" and treating ten events within a single dream rather than sixteen separate dreams [Klaus and Hartmann 2007; Meisig 2010]. Similar dream-interpretation motifs occur elsewhere in Indian literature, such as the *Mahābhārata*, the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, and the *Kalīla wa-Dimna* / *Bidpai* fables [Burlingame 1921; Klaus and Hartmann 2007]. In material culture, eight consecutive reliefs at Borobudur (balustrade IIB-81 to IIB-88) depict the *Mahāsupinajātaka* in close agreement with the Pali narrative, and modern Sinhalese *toraṇa* gateway art in Kandy likewise portrays the king's sixteen dreams in distinct panels [Fontein 2012; Appleton 2010]. DharmaNexus records text reuse within the Pali tradition between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (longest match spanning segments 0.4–2.3), with no automated cross-language matches above the reporting threshold [DharmaNexus].
